pedagogy_description: How PyDA Course teaches programming and data analysis: the lesson loop, the math-first derivations, the short lessons, and the game layer, explained for teachers and students.
pedagogy_intro_1: This course was built on one question: how does a beginner actually learn to program? The answer shapes every lesson, every quiz, and every point on the progress bar.
pedagogy_intro_2: This page explains the design in plain terms, so teachers can see what is happening under the hood, and so can students. Nothing here happens behind their back.
pedagogy_core_lede: Every lesson runs the same loop that working programmers live in: meet a problem, derive a tool, run it, then check what stuck.
pedagogy_core_hook: A hook, often mathematical. Each lesson opens from a concrete pattern you already half-know: an arithmetic sequence, a function rule, a set. It is a place to stand.
pedagogy_core_derive: Concepts are built step by step in prose and code, nothing is asserted before it is earned, so the 'why' is never an afterthought.
pedagogy_core_run: Code you can run immediately. Every code snippet executes in the browser. There is no wall between reading and doing, and running is a click, never a setup.
pedagogy_core_check: A check that costs nothing. Each lesson ends with a low-stakes quiz with instant feedback, plus challenges that reward working the answer out before revealing it.
pedagogy_anatomy_lede: Open any lesson and you will meet the same five moves, in the same order:
pedagogy_anatomy_1: Narrative sections that derive each idea step by step before naming it.
pedagogy_anatomy_2: Short, runnable examples that show the idea working. Every one of them executes.
pedagogy_anatomy_3: 🧩 Challenges: think first, then reveal. The answer stays folded until you have actually tried.
pedagogy_anatomy_4: Socratic questions that ask you to re-derive the idea rather than recall it.
pedagogy_anatomy_5: A quick-check quiz with instant, judgment-free feedback.
pedagogy_short_lede: Short lessons are deliberate. Each lasts around fifteen minutes, because knowledge sticks better in small, regular doses than in rare marathon sessions.
pedagogy_short_1: One concept per lesson. Each lesson teaches one idea deeply instead of five ideas shallowly.
pedagogy_short_2: Fifteen minutes fits a daily habit. Short enough to finish, short enough to repeat tomorrow, which is exactly the rhythm the streak system encourages.
pedagogy_short_3: Frequent beats long. Five short returns build more durable knowledge than one marathon sitting.
pedagogy_short_4: Depth is a spiral. Ideas first met in a short lesson return in richer form in later lessons, modules, and projects.
pedagogy_spiral_lede: The course is a spiral curriculum: you meet an idea, revisit it with more depth, and finally use it in something real.
pedagogy_spiral_py: Python 101, the foundation: printing and variables, then operators, control flow, functions, strings, data structures, and file I/O. Each short lesson builds directly on the last.
pedagogy_spiral_da: Data Analysis with real data in pandas: Series and DataFrames, selection and filtering, cleaning, group-by, and a complete Titanic exploration.
pedagogy_spiral_projects: Guided projects. Each one reuses earlier skills in a realistic build, so the spiral closes with practice instead of repetition.
pedagogy_math_lede: PyDA stands for Python + Data Analysis, but the glue between them is mathematical thinking. The lessons borrow mathematicians' most useful notations, so that programming becomes applied math literacy:
pedagogy_math_1: Sequences ↔ loops. range(n) is the arithmetic progression a, a+d, a+2d, …
pedagogy_math_2: Functions ↔ Python functions. f(x) = x² − 5x + 6 is a rule on parameters, and add(a, b) is the same idea in code.
pedagogy_math_3: Set-builder notation ↔ comprehensions. {x² | x ∈ {1,2,3}} is almost literal Python.
pedagogy_math_4: Half-open intervals ↔ slicing. s[a:b] behaves exactly like the interval [a, b), and there is a reason: it makes slices compose cleanly.
pedagogy_assess_lede: Quizzes are formative. A wrong answer costs nothing, it only feeds a game-style 'death' in your report. Instant feedback shows the right reasoning on the spot, so a mistake becomes the moment you learn instead of a reason to fear the quiz.
pedagogy_game_lede: XP, ranks, streaks, and quests exist for one reason: motivation. The design follows the evidence in
pedagogy_game_post: (a visual-novel-based computing course measured with N-Gain 0.61 and 87.6% acceptance).
pedagogy_game_body: Numbers only ever accumulate, so nothing can be lost. The game rewards effort without punishing mistakes. XP is earned for any visible action: running code, finishing a lesson, a correct quiz answer, or simply returning on a new day.
pedagogy_growth_lede: The progress page is an exercise in reading your own learning: win rate, K/D/A, farm, streaks, consistency, and diagnostics including an N-Gain equivalent. It is a mirror for self-regulation.
pedagogy_ecology_heading: Where skill comes from: the ecology of talent
pedagogy_ecology_lede: Skill grows inside environments, places where people watch good models, make mistakes on purpose, and get invited to join in. Daniel Coyle's work on deep practice, ignition, and culture shows what makes such environments work. This course applies it feature by feature. Here are the ideas and where each one shows up:
pedagogy_ecology_1: Mistakes are information. Deep practice means feeling the error and reaching again. Every quick check, quiz, and challenge is a low-stakes attempt with instant feedback, tuned so you miss around 20% of the time, the documented sweet spot for learning.
pedagogy_ecology_2: Watch, struggle, borrow. Lessons start with worked examples to study closely, then make you re-derive and rebuild the same idea. Borrowing a pattern you just saw is how working craftsmen learn, and it is encouraged here.
pedagogy_ecology_3: Motivation starts with an invitation. XP, streaks, ranks, and badges are the pull that draws you in. Guided projects and capstones show a possible future self, the horizon that says: if they can do it, why can't I?
pedagogy_ecology_4: The workshop model. Fundamentals are built piece by piece before serious performance, and projects put you to work on real builds. The progress page is the floor plan of the workshop, what is solid and what needs another pass.
pedagogy_privacy_lede: Everything stays in the browser's local storage under a single key. There is no account, no server, and no leaderboard. No data ever leaves the device, which makes the course safe to run in a classroom with zero setup.
pedagogy_teacher_lede: Running the course takes five minutes and a projector:
pedagogy_teacher_1: Assign a path. Python 101 first, then Data Analysis. The learner’s progress page is the class map.
pedagogy_teacher_2: Teach live from the lessons. Every example runs in the browser, so a lesson can become a live demo at any moment.
pedagogy_teacher_3: Use the guided projects as deliverables. Each is a complete, gradeable build, not an exercise.
pedagogy_teacher_4: Treat quizzes as formative. Read their accuracy as a signal of coverage, not as a grade to collect.

guide_description: A step-by-step guide to writing a real-world project for this course and opening your first pull request.
guide_intro: Every real-world project here started as one markdown file in someone's pull request. This page lists exactly what to change, in order, plus the commands to check your work before you submit it.
guide_step_1_body: Before anything else, make sure you have what the project needs. You need Node 22 or newer (the site builds with it) and git. If a command below prints nothing, that tool is missing.
guide_step_1_steps:
node --version
git --version

If Node is older than 22, install the current LTS from nodejs.org before continuing.
guide_step_1_expect:
node --version   # v22.x or newer
git --version    # any recent version
guide_step_2_body: A fork is your own copy of the repository, on your GitHub account. You work there, so nothing you do can affect the live site.
guide_step_2_steps:
Open github.com/abderrahim-lectures/python-data-analysis-course.
Click the Fork button at the top right.
Choose your own account as the destination.
Wait for GitHub to finish copying (a few seconds).
You now have github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/python-data-analysis-course.
guide_step_2_expect: Your browser is on your fork, and the header says "forked from abderrahim-lectures/python-data-analysis-course".
guide_step_3_body: Cloning downloads your fork to your computer so you can edit files normally. Clone your fork, not the original: you cannot push to the original.
guide_step_3_steps:
Open a terminal in the folder where you keep projects.
Run the clone command below, replacing YOUR-USERNAME.
Move into the new folder.
Install the dependencies.
guide_step_4_body: A branch keeps your work separate from main. One branch per project, so a reviewer can see exactly what you changed and nobody else is blocked while it is reviewed.
guide_step_4_steps:
Pick a short name from your project, lowercase with hyphens.
Create and switch to it in one command.
guide_step_5_title: Copy a project as your template
guide_step_5_body: Every project page is a markdown file with the same skeleton. Start from one that already works rather than an empty file: it has the frontmatter, a challenge and a quiz in the right shape.
guide_step_5_steps: Copy ai-agent.md to your project's filename. The filename becomes the URL, so name it what you want the page called.
guide_step_5_expect: src/content/projects/file-organizer.md is created and opens in your editor.
guide_step_6_body: The frontmatter is the block between the two --- lines at the top. Four fields are required: title, description, difficulty and author. The tests reject a project missing any of them.
guide_step_6_steps:
Edit title: what the card shows. Keep it under about 50 characters.
Edit description: one sentence, under about 160 characters, saying what the reader builds.
Set difficulty: exactly beginner, intermediate or advanced.
Set author: your contributor id from step 9. A placeholder is fine for now.
guide_step_6_expect: A frontmatter like the example below. The two --- lines must be the very first and last lines of the block.
guide_step_7_body: The body is what a reader actually follows. Every project in this course has the same shape, so readers know where to look.
guide_step_7_steps:
Start with a # heading and one line on what they will build.
Add a why-this-matters paragraph: the problem before the solution.
Add a numbered What you will do list of 3-6 outcomes.
Break the build into steps, each with a real command and its real output.
Add one challenge with a hidden answer (a <details> block).
Add a short quiz (the <div class="quiz"> block).
guide_step_7_expect: A page that reads like the other project pages: introduction, numbered outcomes, step-by-step build, challenge, quiz.
guide_step_8_body: If your project has code worth running, give it a folder so readers can run it themselves. Projects that are mostly explanation can skip this step entirely.
guide_step_8_steps:
Create examples/<your-slug>/.
Add your code file, for example organizer.py.
Add a README.md explaining how to run it.
Add a pyproject.toml so `uv run` works.
Nothing here needs third-party packages unless the project genuinely requires them.
guide_step_9_body: The contributors page is built from a registry, not from git history, so your name appears only if you add it. This also lets students without a GitHub account be credited.
guide_step_9_steps:
Open src/lib/contributors.ts.
Add one entry to the CONTRIBUTORS array.
Use the same id you put in your project's author field.
Save the file.
guide_step_9_expect: Your entry in the array, exactly like the example below. The id is lowercase with hyphens and must match author exactly.
guide_step_10_body: These are the same checks CI runs. Run them before opening the pull request so a reviewer sees a green build, not a list of errors.
guide_step_10_steps:
npm run test checks the content schema, links and translations.
npx tsc --noEmit checks the TypeScript.
npm run build builds every page, which catches broken imports.
guide_step_10_expect: Tests 1743 passed (38 files). No TypeScript errors. Build complete with no failed pages.
guide_step_11_body: A commit is a save point with a message. A push sends it to your fork on GitHub, where the pull request can see it.
guide_step_11_steps:
Stage the files you changed.
Commit with a short message describing what you added.
Push the branch to your fork.
guide_step_12_body: A pull request asks a maintainer to review your work and merge it. Describe what the project teaches and who it is for; a reviewer reads the content, not just the diff.
guide_step_12_steps:
Go to your fork on GitHub; a banner offers to open a pull request.
Click Compare & pull request.
Write a title and a description using the template below.
Click Create pull request.
guide_step_12_expect: A pull request page showing your changes and the CI checks running.

guide_refs_description: The books the Statistics 101 section is built from, with what each one covers and which lessons it is best for.
guide_refs_link_lede: Five books, and what each one is best for
guide_refs_intro: Every lesson in this section is written from standard sources rather than invented. These are the books behind it, and what each one is genuinely useful for — so when a lesson leaves you wanting more on one topic, you know which to open.
guide_refs_foot: All five are standard undergraduate or practitioner texts. The lesson pages do not cite them inline: the goal is that you can read a lesson without a book open, and reach for one only when you want to go further.
guide_ref_kaptein: The closest match to this course’s approach: statistics as something you do in code. Its chapter on correlation and resampling is the clearest treatment of the topics the other books skip.
guide_ref_peck: A thorough introductory text with a large bank of worked examples. Best for the descriptive half of the course: quartiles, spread and the mechanics of the normal curve.
guide_ref_bruce: Practitioner-oriented and short on theory by design. Best for seeing each idea applied to real data, and the only one here written for people who already write code.
guide_ref_taylor: Measurement-focused and careful about the assumptions behind each technique. Denser than the others, and best once you have the basics.
guide_ref_gillard: A compact, proof-aware undergraduate treatment. Best for understanding why the formulas are what they are, rather than how to compute them.

guide_tips_heading: Things that get a pull request merged faster
guide_tip_1: Teach one thing end to end. A project that builds one small tool honestly beats one that touches five libraries.
guide_tip_2: Keep the code runnable. A reader should be able to copy a step and run it, not just read it.
guide_tip_3: Write the pitfalls section last, from the mistakes you actually made while building it.
guide_tip_4: Do not add a translation yourself unless you actually speak the language. English is enough; translators pick up the rest.
guide_file_project: The project page itself. Frontmatter fields: title, description, difficulty, tags, and author (your contributor id). Everything after the frontmatter is the lesson the reader follows.
guide_file_example: Companion code that a reader can run locally, if the project has code. Projects that teach a concept rather than build a tool can skip it.
guide_file_registry_body: Add an entry with your id, display name, and optionally your GitHub handle. Set author: <your-id> on your project page and it appears on the contributors page.
